Neonates of the Wood lemming emerge weighing approximately 3.2 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.2 grams], a modest birth mass that is typical among small-bodied arvicoline rodents. This initial size belies the rapid developmental trajectory observed in captivity, where pups grow quickly on a rich milk diet provided by the mother. Within the first three weeks of life, the young undergo a substantial transformation, transitioning from entirely dependent newborns to increasingly mobile and exploratory juveniles. Under stable thermal conditions of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], which corresponds to the species typical core body temperature during active metabolic periods, the weaning process concludes quite rapidly; the time since birth at weaning is approximately 20 days since birth [tx = approximately 20 days since birth]. At this point, the offspring, now nutritionally independent, typically have attained a wet weight at weaning of about 15.7 grams [Wwx = about 15.7 grams]. The relatively short duration of the lactation period, compared to other rodents of similar size, may be an adaptation to the brief and unpredictable growing season characteristic of the boreal and subarctic habitats this species occupies. This rapid early development continues as the young proceed through the juvenile phase toward reproductive maturity.

Continuing along the developmental timeline, the onset of sexual maturation in female Wood lemmings occurs relatively early in life. Under the same thermal regime of 39 °C [T = 39 °C] used in laboratory colonies to approximate active body temperature, females achieve puberty at 33 days after birth [tp = 33 days after birth]. This remarkably swift attainment of reproductive capability is among the fastest recorded for any member of the subfamily Arvicolinae and is a critical life-history trait that facilitates rapid population growth during favorable summers. The time from birth to puberty is notably brief, and it allows females born early in the breeding season to potentially contribute offspring within the same calendar year. Following puberty, gestation proceeds rapidly as well. The gestation time for this species is reported as 22 days [tg = 22 days], again measured at a body temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], a duration that is comparatively short and aligns with the pattern of accelerated reproduction seen in many small mammals inhabiting strongly seasonal environments with narrow windows of resource abundance.

The reproductive output of the Wood lemming is characterized by a high potential rate, reflecting its status as a classic r-selected species. Females typically produce litters of 4.6 pups per litter [N_R_i = 4.6 pups per litter]. This fecundity measure alone, however, does not capture the full scope of their productive capacity. When considering the frequency of reproductive events across the breeding season, available data indicate that females can achieve approximately 2 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 litters per year]. The combined annual reproductive rate, inferred from this litter size and frequency, suggests a remarkably high maximum rate of offspring production. This substantial output is a fundamental driver of the population irruptions for which this species is known, allowing numbers to swell dramatically during years of abundant food resources, particularly when their preferred mosses are plentiful. The physiological costs of such intensive reproduction are considerable, and the energy demands on lactating females are extreme during the peak of the breeding season.

Regarding the ultimate body size attained by adults, the Wood lemming reaches a fairly modest adult body mass compared to other members of its guild. The ultimate wet weight for a fully grown individual, measured across both sexes in wild-caught specimens, is approximately 25 grams [Wwi = approximately 25 grams]. This relatively small body size is consistent with their dietary specialization on mosses, which are a low-quality forage material, and likely imposes constraints on their energetic budgets and life-history scheduling. The maximum lifespan for this species, in contrast to its rapid early development, is notably brief. Data regarding longevity remain somewhat uncertain due to the difficulty of tracking individuals in the wild across multiple years, but the best available estimates from both field mark-recapture studies and captive observations suggest that the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 2.1 years [am = approximately 2.1 years] under a thermoneutral body temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. This short lifespan, combined with a high reproductive rate, defines a life-history strategy heavily weighted toward early and prolific breeding rather than somatic persistence.

The compressed life span and high early reproductive investment of the Wood lemming have clear implications for its population dynamics and ecological role. The combination of rapid sexual maturation, a maximized daily reproductive rate derived from the size and frequency of litters, and a short generation time predisposes this species to dramatic population fluctuations. These boom-and-bust cycles are a hallmark of many boreal microtines and are thought to be driven by a complex interplay of food availability, predation pressure, and intrinsic density-dependent factors. The comparatively short gestation period, documented at 22 days [tg = 22 days] at 39 °C [T = 39 °C], and the early age at weaning, recorded at 20 days after birth [tx = 20 days after birth], ensure that each generation turns over rapidly, allowing multiple cohorts to be produced within a single favorable summer. The functional consequences of this pace of life extend beyond demography; they also shape the species role as a keystone prey item for a suite of mammalian and avian predators in taiga ecosystems of Fennoscandia and Siberia. The relatively low birth weight of approximately 3.2 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.2 grams] is rapidly compensated for by a high milk energy content during the pre-weaning phase.
